query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy’s surprisingly low hardness and strength—but good ductility and machinability—are controlled by its high chemical homogeneity that minimizes local chemical short‐range order (CSRO) or nano‐scale precipitate formation. Without such localized compositional modulations, dislocation glide proceeds relatively unimpeded, resulting in low yield strength and hardness. By contrast, alloys that develop CSRO or form nanoscale, Ti‐rich (or other element–rich) precipitates generate dislocation‐pinning obstacles that enhance hardness and strength at the expense of some ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its as-cast single-phase solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: A targeted thermomechanical treatment (for example, an annealing process at an intermediate temperature followed by rapid quenching) intended to induce incipient chemical ordering or the formation of nanoscale precipitates.
generation.conditions: Samples are processed starting with the as-cast state; annealing typically performed at around 600–700 °C (below the melting point) for a controlled time to promote local ordering, then rapidly cooled to room temperature. Mechanical tests are conducted at room temperature under conventional strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of local chemical short‐range order or nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates that act as dislocation pinning sites.
generation.mechanism: The formation of these microstructural obstacles increases the energy barrier for dislocation motion. In the chemically homogeneous starting alloy, dislocations glide easily, resulting in moderate strength and hardness. In the treated alloy, the obstacles frustrate dislocation motion, elevating yield strength and hardness while modestly reducing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast alloy, samples that undergo the treatment should show an appreciable (roughly 20–30% or more) increase in hardness and yield strength, accompanied by a moderate reduction in plastic strain. Microstructural analysis should reveal the presence of local ordering or nanoscale precipitates correlated with the enhanced hardness and strength.
generation.baseline: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple single-phase solid-solution state exhibits relatively low hardness and strength, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies specifically to equimolar (or near-equimolar) CoCrFeNiTi in the single-phase state; if additional phases develop or if processing exceeds the recommended temperature and time windows, the effect may be altered or overshadowed by other strengthening mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise treatment conditions required to reproducibly induce the optimal degree of CSRO or precipitate formation and the quantitative impact on dislocation interactions remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi specimens: one group retained in the as-cast state (control) and one group subjected to the defined thermomechanical treatment intended to induce local chemical ordering/nanoprecipitation. Characterize both groups using TEM, XRD, and possibly atom probe tomography to assess the presence of local ordering. Then, perform mechanical tests (nanoindentation, tensile measurements) to compare hardness, yield strength, and plastic strain.
measurements: Microstructural imaging (TEM, APT) to confirm or refute the formation of local chemical order/nanoprecipitates
Tensile yield strength and plastic strain from standardized tests
Dislocation density and slip behavior observations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanical treatment does not produce a detectable increase in local chemical ordering or nanoprecipitate formation, or if the treated samples do not exhibit at least a 10–20% increase in hardness and yield strength relative to the control while showing changes in dislocation behavior consistent with increased pinning, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The Effect of Electronic Structure on the Phases Present in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractMulticomponent systems, termed High Entropy Alloys (HEAs), with predominantly single solid solution phases are a current area of focus in alloy development. Although different empirical rules have been introduced to understand phase formation and determine what the dominant phases may be in these systems, experimental investigation has revealed that in many cases their structure is not a single solid solution phase, and that the rules may not accurately distinguish the stability of the phase boundaries. Here, a combined modelling and experimental approach that looks into the electronic structure is proposed to improve accuracy of the predictions of the majority phase. To do this, the Rigid Band model is generalised for magnetic systems in prediction of the majority phase most likely to be found. Good agreement is found when the predictions are confronted with data from experiments, including a new magnetic HEA system (CoFeNiV). Nanoindentation behavior of high entropy alloys with transformation-induced plasticity

Abstract: Nanoindentation of three metastable dual-phase high entropy alloys (HEAs) was performed to obtain their inherent elastoplastic deformation responses. Excellent combination of hardness and elastic modulus in as-cast condition confirmed that, their inherently higher strength compared to other HEAs reported in literature, can be attributed to alloy chemistry induced phase stability. Further, hardness of 8.28 GPa combined with modulus of 221.8 GPa was obtained in Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Cu HEA by annealing the as-cast material, which is the best hardness-modulus combination obtained to date in HEAs from nanoindentation. On the other hand, although Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si HEA showed lower hardness and modulus than Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Al and Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Cu HEAs, the former alloy exhibited the highest strain rate sensitivity, as determined from tests performed at five different strain rates. Strength can be controlled by edge dislocations in refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractEnergy efficiency is motivating the search for new high-temperature (high-T) metals. Some new body-centered-cubic (BCC) random multicomponent “high-entropy alloys (HEAs)” based on refractory elements (Cr-Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W-Hf-Ti-Zr) possess exceptional strengths at high temperatures but the physical origins of this outstanding behavior are not known. Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations. This finding is surprising because plastic flows in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations.
